form: Locative Demonstratives in nɬeʔkepmxcín * Reed Steiner University of British Columbia Abstract: This paper reexamines the demonstrative paradigm of nɬeʔkepmxcín, and finds that what Thompson and Thompson (1992:134-137) describe as a homogenous class can actually be subdi- vided into two kinds of demonstratives. Demonstratives associated with nouns are labeled demon- strative pronouns following work by van Eijk (1997) on St’át’imcets, and are set aside for this paper. Demonstratives that modify the location of an individual or event are labeled locative demonstra- tives following Koch (2008b:67-68). The main argument of this paper is that locative demonstra- tives are lexicalized prepositional phrases, consisting of a preposition with a deictic complement. They are modeled under a vector-based framework that builds on Zwarts and Winter (2000). The spatial trace function of Link (1998) and Krifka (1989, 1998) is generalized to individuals in lieu of separate Loc and anti-Loc functions, and a novel “Follows” function is assumed for directing events along paths.
Keywords: nɬeʔkepmxcín, Salish, demonstratives, deixis, prepositions, vectors

form: There are two main empirical findings outlined in this paper. The first finding is that there are two classes of demonstratives in nɬeʔkepmxcín: a nominal class (‘demonstrative pronouns’, follow- ing van Eijk 1997) and an adverbial class (‘locative demonstratives’, following comments in Koch 2008b:67-68). The second finding is that the adverbial demonstratives have the same syntactic and semantic properties as prepositional phrases with deictic complements (see Thompson and Thompson 1992:137). Neither finding is cross-linguistically surprising, but both findings chal- lenge how the paradigm is organized in existing literature (Thompson and Thompson 1992:135- 137).

form: nɬeʔkepmxcín is a Northern Interior Salish language spoken in the British Columbia Interior, along the Thompson, Fraser, and Nicola rivers (Thompson and Thompson 1992:ix). As of the most recent FPCC report (Gessner, Herbert, and Parker 2022), there are currently about 100 fluent first-language speakers, most of whom are elderly (for details on the status of nɬeʔkepmxcín, see Gessner et al. 2022:51). Many communities are actively engaged in revitalizing the language. Like first-language (L1) speakers of any natural human language, L1 speakers of nɬeʔkep- mxcín have sophisticated, subconscious knowledge of how to use their language. They can intu- itively judge if a sentence sounds well-formed or ill-formed in any given context, even if they’ve never heard the sentence before and never been taught ‘the rules’. Such judgements are a cru- cial resource for linguistic research and language documentation. By supplying L1 speakers with sentences in a carefully controlled contexts, then asking for their judgements, it is possible to reconstruct how a language works ‘under the hood’.

form: There is a large, although closed, nonproductive, class of deictic words. The organiza- tion of the system is poorly understood at this writing, as are the semantic limits and usage of the words themselves. The borderline between demonstratives and words of more locative flavor is hazy, although they are here separated for presentation. They are extremely common, both in narrative texts and in everyday conversation, which is part of what makes it so difficult to establish their basic meanings, to say nothing of their special uses. There also seems to be a great deal of dialectal variation in both forms and meanings in this category. (Thompson and Thompson 1992:134) Although nɬeʔkepmxcín has a distinct paradigm, there are systematic syntactic and semantic similarities to demonstratives in other Salish languages, e.g. St’át’imcets (a.k.a. Lillooet, ISO 639-3: lil) (Matthewson 2022a; Matthewson and Davis 1995) and ʔayʔaǰuθəm (a.k.a. Comox- Sliammon; ISO 639-3: coo) (Reisinger and Huijsmans 2021). These similarities will be discussed throughout the paper.

In sum, there is little literature on demonstratives in nɬeʔkepmxcín, but there is a wealth of theoretical literature on demonstratives in other Salish languages. Together, these two bodies of research inform the diagnostic tests used throughout this paper.
3 Two kinds of demonstratives in nɬeʔkepmxcín

2 Three of the morphemes that Thompson and Thompson (1992) identify as demonstratives are excluded from this list. One such morpheme is the polar question predicate kéʔe, which Thompson and Thompson suggest has a second usage as an indefinite pronoun. However, they provide no examples of this usage, and neither I nor Matthewson (2023:291) have been able to elicit it.

In total, there are at least ten demonstratives in nɬeʔkepmxcín.2 Thompson and Thompson (1992) group them into a single homogenous class, which this paper subdivides into two subclasses: demonstrative pronouns (Section 3.1) and locative demonstratives (Section 3.2).3 As a general- ization, demonstrative pronouns are associated with individuals, whereas locative demonstratives are generally associated with event locations. The distinction between these two gorups will be discussed in the following subsections.

form: xʔé ‘this, these’ is proximal: it relates to an individual relatively close to the speaker – usually within arm’s reach (Mandy Jimmie, p.c.). xéʔe ‘that, those’ is distal: it relates to an individual fur- ther away from the speaker. Both of these demonstratives are extremely common. The remaining two DemPNs encode evidence, the precise details of which require further research. ɬǝ́n̕e ‘this, that (no longer present)’ relates to someone or something absent from the conversation, usually having just departed. I hypothesize it encodes previous direct evidence, like ɬɛn̓ in ʔayʔaǰuθəm (Reisinger and Huijsmans 2021). kʷukʷ usually relates to something unseen. Both evidential demonstratives occur in all dialects tested, although they are less common than xʔé and xéʔe. The DemPNs of nɬeʔkepmxcín are presented in Table 1.

3 A subset of demonstratives from both subclasses appear at the end of the second position clitic string (see Thompson and Thompson 1992:139-142). It is likely that some of these cases do involve cliticization, but there is not yet a reliable test to distinguish clitic demonstratives from non-clitic demonstratives in nɬeʔkepmxcín. Although clitic demonstratives are well attested in other Salish languages (Huijsmans 2023; Matthewson and Davis 1995), the same tests do not apply to nɬeʔkepmxcín. Word order is not an entirely reliable test here because subjects are allowed in the same position (see Koch 2006b:110 footnote 9). Stress is not a reliable test, either, because clitics in nɬeʔkepmxcín are outside the primary stress domain (Hall, Luntzlara, Mellesmoen, and Reid 2025). A working hypothesis is that distal demonstratives are clitics when they lose their final vowel, e.g. when xéʔe is pronounced as xeʔ. This final-vowel loss is not well understood in the literature on nɬeʔkepmxcín, but in ʔayʔaǰuθəm, clausal demonstrative clitics resemble regular demonstratives without the final vowel. It could be the case, then, that loss of the final vowel in nɬeʔkepmxcín is associated with clitic versions of corresponding demonstratives, but this requires testing. For simplicity, this paper leaves cliticization to future research.

form: DemPNs appear in argument positions and form constituents with DPs (Section 3.1.1). Like DPs, they resist unmarked in-situ adjunction (Section 3.1.2) and resist predication (Section 3.1.3), and they are focused using a clefting copula ʔé or c̕é (Section 3.1.4). This paper analyzes them as DPs (Section 3.1.5).
In general, DemPNs pattern like determiner phrases (DPs). They are permitted as independent arguments so long as the context is explicit enough that the referent is unambiguous (1).4

form: While it is true that second-position DemPNs are not necessarily arguments, it is also un- likely that they are locative adjuncts on the predicate, since they contribute zero locative seman- tics. Koch (2008b) hypothesizes that they function as discourse-level situation deictics. This would make them similar to clausal demonstratives, like those found in ʔayʔaǰuθəm (Reisinger and Huijsmans 2021). More research is needed to test this hypothesis.

Clausal demonstratives are beyond the scope of this paper, but they are important to flag for elicitation purposes. If clausal demonstratives always surface in second position, as in ʔayʔaǰuθəm (Huijsmans 2023; Reisinger and Huijsmans 2021), then they follow the predicate when no aux- iliary is present. As a result, a post-predicative demonstrative in a clause without an auxiliary is ambiguous between a clausal demonstrative and a non-clausal demonstrative. For this reason, auxiliaries should always be used to disambiguate between clausal and non-clausal demonstratives when eliciting acceptability judgements on demonstratives.
Assuming non-argument demonstratives in second-position are clausal demonstratives, the generalization holds that DemPNs must be arguments; they cannot be adjuncts to the predicate.

The remaining six demonstratives in nɬeʔkepmxcín are locative demonstratives (LocDems), which relate to locations instead of individuals. The distinction between nominal demonstratives (DemPNs) and adverbial demonstratives (LocDems) is not cross-linguistically surprising, but it does differ from existing literature on the language. Recall that Thompson and Thompson (1992) treat all demonstratives as a single ho- mogenous category. Such a paradigm is not descriptively adequate; it is syntactically necessary to subdivide the paradigm into DemPNs and LocDems.

So far, this paper has shown that LocDems are locative adjuncts, but it has not yet shown that LocDems are PPs. The purpose of this section is to show that LocDems systematically pattern like corresponding PPs.

4.1 Basic resemblances between LocDems and PPs

LocDems closely resemble PPs with corresponding meanings. This was first noted in the litera- ture by Thompson and Thompson (1992), who noticed that the first consonant of each demonstra- tive closely resembles some other morpheme in the language. Because Thompson and Thompson do not distinguish DemPNs from LocDems, they are unable to make any generalizations, and they admit that “semantic relationships seem tenuous and unsystematic” (Thompson and Thompson 1992:135). However, once LocDems are distinguished from DemPNs, a systematic pattern does emerge: the initial consonant of each LocDem matches an existing preposition in the language, in both form and function.

To illustrate, Table 5 presents each LocDem with its corresponding preposition. In each case, LocDems denote the same kinds of locations as PPs headed by their corresponding preposition, i.e. n-initial LocDems relate to fairly precise locations and points of contact, t-initial LocDems relate to general areas and regions, and w-intial LocDems relate to the goal of a direction or path.

4.2 LocDems have the same distribution as PPs

Further evidence that LocDems are PPs is that both have the same basic distribution. LocDems and PPs with deictic complements are permitted and rejected in the same syntactic positions. Like LocDems (see Section 3.2.1), other PPs with deictic complements are permitted after the predicate, or between a predicate and its auxiliary. More research is needed to determine the semantic differences between these positions, which may provide insight into second-position LocDems, too. But at least syntactically, PPs and LocDems have the same basic distribution. In (41a), a PP with a deictic complement is permitted post-predicatively and in second position, i.e. the same basic positions as a LocDem.

4.3 The deictic component of a LocDem can be modified directly

So far, it has been shown that LocDems bear a strong phonological and semantic resemblance to PPs, and that they have the same external distribution as prepositions with deictic complements. While this is evidence that there may be a historical relationship between LocDems and PPs, and that both are of the same syntactic category, it does not necessarily show that LocDems can be synchronically segmented into a preposition head and a deictic complement.

What this subsection argues is that the deictic component of a LocDem (i.e. proximal ʔé and distal éʔe) can be modified independently of the prepositional component (i.e. n, t, or w). If this is correct, then LocDems must be synchronically segmentable.

Instead, this paper suggests that the anti-uniqueness presupposition is associated with the deictic component of the LocDem rather than the preposition. Obliques adjoin directly to the deictic component, rather than to the maximal projection of the LocDem. This results in an interpretation where the oblique cannot be unique.

When this evidence is considered in the context of the larger body of data presented in this paper, the similarity between PPs and LocDems becomes striking: they have the basic phono- logical form and semantic function of PPs, they have the external syntax of PPs, and they have the internal syntax of PPs. The simplest conclusion, then, is that LocDems are PPs. The initial consonant is a preposition. The rest of the LocDem is some kind of locative deictic or DemPN, likely somehow related to xʔé ‘this, these’ and xéʔe ‘that, those’, although the exact nature of this relationship is unclear.

form: The first analytical benefit is a more complete paradigm: all four prepositions have a corre- sponding proximal and distal LocDem. The alternative analysis is that tw= ‘from’ is the only preposition which selects xʔé ‘this/these’ or xéʔe ‘that/those’ as a complement and is also the only preposition that lacks corresponding LocDems.

The second analytical benefit is that it provides a way of explaining the irregular morphology associated with tuxʷʔé and tuxʷéʔe, which exceptionally require nominalized remnants in focus contexts instead of subjunctive ones (for discussion, see Hall and Phillips 2024:154-155). This irregularity can be more easily explained if tuxʷʔé and tuxʷéʔe are PPs that have lexicalized into LocDems. Their lexical entries could include some arbitrary feature absent from the preposition itself, which triggers the irregular morphology.

Having established that LocDems are PPs, this section provides a formal semantic analysis. The immediate goals of this analysis are twofold: first, to show that the meaning of each LocDem can be derived from PPs, and second, to model how those PPs relate to the phrases they modify. The analysis builds upon the vector space semantics (VSS) of Zwarts (1997) and Zwarts and Winter (2000), and makes novel ontological claims about the relationship between eventualities and the space they occupy.

form: Prepositions in nɬeʔkepmxcín are modeled under the VSS of Zwarts (1997) and Zwarts and Winter (2000), which represents spatial objects as sets of vectors (Section 5.1.1). Locative prepositions take an input (e.g. an individual, location, or situation) and returns the characteristic function of a set of vectors, which gets type-shifted into a property of individuals or eventualities in adjunct positions (Section 5.1.3). Path prepositions similarly return the characteristic function of a set of vectors, but get type-shifted into a property of events (Section 5.1.4).

In the literature on locative expressions, it is generally agreed that prepositions indicate a spatial relationship. Locative prepositions (e.g. English at, on, under) relate two objects in space: a figure (located object, locatum) and a ground (reference object, relatum, landmark) (Talmy 1985). For instance, in the English DP the cat on the table, the cat is the figure and the table is the ground. By contrast, path prepositions (e.g. toward, from) relate an event’s direction to an object: usually a source (start, beginning, origin), a goal (end, destination), or a route (intermediate path). For instance, in the English sentence they’re going from the river to the sea via the path, the river is the source of the going event, the sea is the goal, and the path is the route. The most common approach to spatial semantics involves a mixed ontology of regions (for locative PPs) and paths (for path PPs). A region is usually modeled as an atomic type (Cohn, Bennett, Gooday, and Gotts 1997; Creary, Gawron, and Nerbonne 1989) or as a set of points (Kracht 2002), but both approaches struggle to account for measured PPs (see Zwarts 1997). A path can be modeled as an atomic type (Krifka 1998), but is more often modeled as an ordered set of points (Bierwisch 1988) or as a function from an interval [0,1] to a position in a one-dimensional stretch of space (Cresswell 1978; Zwarts 2005).

Instead, this paper uses a VSS approach to spatial semantics (Zwarts 1997; Zwarts and Winter 2000).22 A VSS approach models spatial relationships using vectors: directed line segments (Zwarts and Winter 2000).

form: VSS has three analytical advantages for nɬeʔkepmxcín, listed here. (i) Only VSS can com- positionally handle measured PPs like six inches above the table or twelve parsecs from the finish line (for arguments, see Zwarts 1997). nɬeʔkepmxcín does have measure phrases (Givens 2023), so VSS remains a safer bet even if the precise syntax of measure phrases in nɬeʔkepmxcín differs from Germanic languages like English and Dutch. (ii) VSS explains linguistic universals, e.g. it constrains what regions a locative expression can denote and predicts which PPs can be modified (Zwarts and Winter 2000). This makes VSS useful even for languages without measure phrases. (iii) VSS can be extended beyond spatial semantics. Applied to nɬeʔkepmxcín, this has applications for the semantics of comparatives (Davis and Mellesmoen 2019; Faller 2000) and clausal demonstratives (Huijsmans 2023; Reisinger and Huijsmans 2021). See Section 6 for further discussion.

A vector is a directed line segment; it has a magnitude (distance, length) and a direction. The location where a vector begins is its origin or starting point. The location where it ends is its endpoint.

For ease, this paper assumes a semantic type of vectors, written as an up arrow ↑ to avoid confusion with Davidsonian eventualities of type v. Variables of this type are written with a rightward arrow diacritic, e.g. ⃗v or ⃗w.

The semantics of prepositions developed thus far can be extended easily to LocDems; all that is needed is some sort of complement that encodes deictic distance: a proximal complement ʔé and a distal complement éʔe. form: It is unlikely that the labialized fricative /xʷ/ comes from the deictic or determiner; a simpler explanation is that the preposition has an allomorph ending in a labialized fricative, which is only triggered before certain morphemes. An alternative analysis would require the relevant deictic or determiner to begin with a labialized fricative /xʷ/, but the phonological conditions that would trigger its surfacing would also be true of the preposition w= ‘to’, which does not experience the same allomorphy.

What this shows is that analyzing LocDems as PPs with deictic complements predicts and explains an ambiguity that exists independently in the language. Both tw=xʔé ‘from this/these’ and tw=ʔé ‘from here’ surface as tuxʷʔe, and both tw=xéʔe ‘from that/those’ and tw=éʔe ‘from there’ surface as tuxʷéʔe. This supports an insight from Mandy Jimmie (p.c.) that the locative cases do not have DemPN complements.
This section summarizes the paper and examines possible extensions of this research.

form: nɬeʔkpemxcín has two kinds of demonstratives: demonstrative pronouns (DemPNs), which relate to individuals and form constituents with DPs, and locative demonstratives (LocDems), which are primarily locative adjuncts. This is not cross-linguistically surprising, but it does challenge how the deictic paradigm is organized in existing literature on the language (see e.g. Thompson and Thompson 1992). This paper also finds that LocDems have the same distributional and semantic properties as corresponding PPs with deictic complements: nʔé ‘(right) here’ and néʔe ‘(right) there’ correspond to n= ‘at, on. in’; tʔé ‘about here’ and téʔe ‘about there’ correspond to t= ‘by, about’; wʔé and wéʔe correspond to w= ‘to, toward’. These LocDems, as well as the PPs tuxʷʔé ‘from here, from this/these’ and tuxʷéʔe ‘from there, from that/those’ get a unified analysis as PPs with deictic complements. Such PPs are modeled under a vector-based semantics, building on Zwarts (1997) and Zwarts and Winter (2000). To capture the full empirical landscape, it proves useful to bundle the eigenspace function (Wunderlich 1991; Zwarts 1997; Zwarts and Winter 2000) and the spatial trace function (Krifka 1989, 1998; Link 1998) into a single function for mapping inputs to spatial objects. It is also necessary to develop a function for mapping events to paths, such that the event unfolds along the path.

For most purposes, it is more than sufficient to represent LocDems using the simpler denotations that abstract over the vectors. However, this does not mean that the more detailed spatial denota- tions are unnecessary: they are particularly useful for explaining non-spatial extensions of spatial morphemes.

form: With a detailed enough semantics of locatives, it is possible to explain this relationship be- tween spatial morphemes and degree morphemes. Building on Faller (2000), degree adjectives are treated as comparisons between two vectors: a d(imensional)-vector, which represents the degree to which an individual possesses a property, and a u(nit)-vector, which can be understood as a dimension in conceptual space (see Gärdenfors 2000). The benefit to this approach is that antonyms, like ‘tall’ and ‘short’, can be modeled as positive or negative vectors on the same scale. Assuming that the spatial trace function σ returns all vectors associated with its input, including non-spatial ones, then a source PP like tw= ‘from’ can turn a degree adjective into a comparative with no additional semantic machinery, as in (98).

form: A detailed semantics of LocDems may provide insight into how clausal demonstratives work. In their basic spatial use, LocDems relate to positions, distances, and directions in physical space. By hypothesis, clausal demonstratives may relate to positions, distances, and directions between spatiotemporal slices of worlds. More research is needed, but the generalization is that a detailed baseline understanding of how locative semantivs works can generalize to non-locative extensions of those same morphemes.

Finally, this research explains why some Salish languages can (or cannot) permit PPs as pred- icates. Although nominal and adjectival predicates are well attested across Salish (Davis 2022; Kinkade 1983; van Eijk 1997), the status of PP predicates is less clear: they are marginally accept- able in at least some languages (Kroeber 1999:60-62), although at least in nɬeʔkepmxcín, these structures are relatively marked, and their acceptability varies between speakers. This would be surprising if PPs were of type ⟨e, t⟩ or ⟨v, t⟩, because they would be of the same semantic type as an adjectival predicate.

The analysis proposed in this paper, however, suggests that PPs are fundamentally functions of type ⟨↑, t⟩, and must be type-shifted into type ⟨e, t⟩ or ⟨v, t⟩ (following Zwarts 1997; Zwarts and Winter 2000). This is useful for explaining PP predication: speakers who allow PP predicates can coerce PPs into type ⟨v, t⟩ in predicate positions; speakers who reject PP predicates can only coerce PPs in adjunct positions.
